EdgeCase offers several ways to put nodes and edges into a graph, from adding them one at a time to
building a whole graph from a table in one call. This page covers each of them, along with the
methods for deleting nodes and edges and for cleaning up a graph once it's built.

| Task | Methods |
|---|---|
| Add one node or edge | [`add_node()`](../reference/Graph.add_node.qmd), [`add_edge()`](../reference/Graph.add_edge.qmd) |
| Add many nodes or edges | [`add_nodes()`](../reference/Graph.add_nodes.qmd), [`add_edges()`](../reference/Graph.add_edges.qmd) |
| Add edges between node IDs | [`add_edge_by_id()`](../reference/Graph.add_edge_by_id.qmd), [`add_edges_by_id()`](../reference/Graph.add_edges_by_id.qmd) |
| Build a graph from an edge list | [`Graph.from_edges()`](../reference/Graph.from_edges.qmd) |
| Build a graph from DataFrames | [`Graph(nodes_df=, edges_df=)`](../reference/Graph.qmd) |
| Remove nodes or edges | [`delete_node()`](../reference/Graph.delete_node.qmd), [`delete_edge()`](../reference/Graph.delete_edge.qmd), [`delete_edge_by_id()`](../reference/Graph.delete_edge_by_id.qmd) |
| Make a graph simple | [`remove_selfloops()`](../reference/Graph.remove_selfloops.qmd), [`remove_duplicate_edges()`](../reference/Graph.remove_duplicate_edges.qmd), [`simplify()`](../reference/Graph.simplify.qmd) |

Every one of these methods changes the graph in place and returns it, so they chain freely, and
each call is recorded as a step in the graph's [step log](step-log.qmd).

## Adding nodes

### One at a time

[`add_node()`](../reference/Graph.add_node.qmd) adds a single node. Its first argument is the
label, `type=` sets the node's type, and any other keyword argument becomes an attribute:

```{python}
import edgecase as ec

lab = (
    ec.Graph()
    .add_node("Curie", type="scientist", field="chemistry", born=1867)
    .add_node("Bohr", type="scientist", field="physics", born=1885)
    .add_node("Solvay 1911", type="conference")
)
lab.get_node_df()
```

`add_node()` can also connect the new node to an existing one as it is created. Note the direction
of the two arguments, which is easy to get backwards: `from_node=` makes an edge *from the new
node to* the given node, and `to_node=` makes an edge *from the given node to* the new one. In an
undirected graph the direction doesn't matter:

```{python}
tree = (
    ec.Graph(directed=True)
    .add_node("root")
    .add_node("child", to_node="root")
    .add_node("grandchild", to_node="child")
)
tree.get_edges_str_repr()
```

Each string in the result reads `source->target` with node IDs, so the edges run from the root
(ID 1) to the child (ID 2), and from the child to the grandchild (ID 3).

### Many at once

[`add_nodes()`](../reference/Graph.add_nodes.qmd) takes a list (or any iterable) of labels. A
`type=` or other keyword argument given to it applies to every node in the call:

```{python}
team = ec.Graph().add_nodes(["Ines", "Jon", "Kai"], type="engineer", team="platform")
team.get_node_df()
```

When some nodes need their own values, give those nodes as `(label, attributes)` tuples. The
dictionary is merged over the shared attributes, and may include a `"type"` key:

```{python}
team.add_nodes(
    ["Lena", ("Max", {"team": "data"}), ("Nia", {"type": "manager"})],
    type="engineer",
    team="platform",
)
team.get_node_df()
```

A dictionary from labels to attribute dictionaries works too, which is a natural fit for data
loaded from JSON. Use `None` for a node with no attributes:

```{python}
ec.Graph().add_nodes({"x": {"size": 3}, "y": {"size": 5}, "z": None}).get_node_df()
```

A `range` adds nodes labelled with numbers, converted to strings:

```{python}
ec.Graph().add_nodes(range(1, 4)).get_node_df()
```

## Adding edges

### One at a time

[`add_edge()`](../reference/Graph.add_edge.qmd) joins a source to a target, given as labels or
IDs. `rel=` sets the relationship type, `weight=` the weight, and other keywords become edge
attributes:

```{python}
lab.add_edge("Curie", "Solvay 1911", rel="attended")
lab.add_edge("Bohr", "Curie", rel="corresponded", weight=3, topic="radioactivity")
lab.get_edge_df()
```

By default, both endpoints must already exist, which catches typos in labels. Pass
`auto_create_nodes=True` to have `add_edge()` create any missing node (given as a label) on the
spot:

```{python}
lab.add_edge("Einstein", "Solvay 1911", rel="attended", auto_create_nodes=True)
lab.get_node_df()
```

Einstein was created without a type or any other attributes, which can be set afterwards with
the methods in [Node and edge data](node-and-edge-data.qmd).

### Many at once

[`add_edges()`](../reference/Graph.add_edges.qmd) takes a list of edges, each of which can have one
of four shapes:

| Shape | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `(source, target)` | a plain edge |
| `(source, target, weight)` | an edge with a weight |
| `(source, target, attrs)` | an edge with attributes, where `attrs` may include `"rel"` and `"weight"` |
| `(source, target, weight, attrs)` | both |

The shapes can be mixed in one list. As with `add_nodes()`, keyword arguments set values shared by
every edge, which an edge's own dictionary overrides:

```{python}
flights = (
    ec.Graph(directed=True, weighted=True)
    .add_nodes(["YVR", "SEA", "SFO", "LAX"])
    .add_edges(
        [
            ("YVR", "SEA", 190),
            ("SEA", "SFO", 1093),
            ("SFO", "LAX", 543, {"airline": "Alaska"}),
            ("YVR", "LAX", {"weight": 1745, "rel": "nonstop"}),
        ],
        rel="route",
        airline="United",
    )
)
flights.get_edge_df()
```

The weights here are distances in kilometers, so on this weighted graph the shortest route from
Vancouver to Los Angeles is the nonstop flight, at 1745 km, rather than the 1826 km of hops down
the coast:

```{python}
flights.shortest_path_length("YVR", "LAX")
```

### Edges between node IDs

`add_edge()` and `add_edges()` accept IDs as well as labels, following the usual rule that an `int`
is an ID and a `str` a label. When edges come from code that works with IDs, such as the `id`
column of a node table or the result of an algorithm,
[`add_edge_by_id()`](../reference/Graph.add_edge_by_id.qmd) and
[`add_edges_by_id()`](../reference/Graph.add_edges_by_id.qmd) are a stricter choice: they accept
only integers, and raise a `TypeError` if a label slips in.

```{python}
ring = ec.Graph().add_nodes(["a", "b", "c", "d"])
ids = ring.get_node_df()["id"].to_list()

ring.add_edges_by_id([(ids[i], ids[(i + 1) % len(ids)]) for i in range(len(ids))])
ring.get_edges_str_repr()
```

## Building a graph from an edge list

Often the edges are all there is: a list of pairs read from a file or produced by another program.
[`Graph.from_edges()`](../reference/Graph.from_edges.qmd) builds a whole graph from such a list in
one call. Every endpoint becomes a node, in order of first appearance, so there's no need to create
the nodes first:

```{python}
citations = ec.Graph.from_edges(
    [("paper_a", "paper_b"), ("paper_a", "paper_c"), ("paper_b", "paper_c"), ("paper_d", "paper_a")],
    directed=True,
    graph_name="Citations",
)
citations
```

The edge tuples take the same four shapes as in `add_edges()`. The graph is made weighted
automatically when any edge has a weight, unless `weighted=` says otherwise.

Every endpoint is read as a label, even when it's a number: `from_edges([(0, 1), (1, 2)])` gives
nodes labelled `"0"`, `"1"` and `"2"`, with IDs 1, 2 and 3. Use `nodes=` to add nodes that have no
edges, to give nodes attributes, or to control which IDs the nodes receive. It takes any of the
forms that `add_nodes()` accepts, and its nodes are created first:

```{python}
ec.Graph.from_edges(
    [(1, 2), (2, 3)],
    nodes=[("0", {"isolated": True}), "1", "2", "3"],
).get_node_df()
```

## Building a graph from DataFrames

Tabular data maps onto a graph naturally: one table of nodes and one of edges. The `Graph`
constructor accepts both as Polars DataFrames.

- In `nodes_df=`, the `id` column holds each node's label (the node IDs are still assigned by
  EdgeCase). If the table also has a `label` column, that column is used for the labels instead. A
  `type` column sets node types, and every other column becomes an attribute.
- In `edges_df=`, the `from` and `to` columns hold the labels of each edge's endpoints. A `weight`
  column sets weights, a `rel` column sets relationship types, and every other column becomes an
  attribute.

```{python}
import polars as pl

stations = pl.DataFrame({
    "id": ["Central", "Harbour", "Museum", "Park"],
    "type": ["interchange", "terminal", "stop", "stop"],
    "zone": [1, 1, 1, 2],
})

lines = pl.DataFrame({
    "from": ["Central", "Central", "Museum"],
    "to": ["Harbour", "Museum", "Park"],
    "rel": ["blue_line", "red_line", "red_line"],
    "weight": [4.0, 2.5, 6.0],
})

transit = ec.Graph(nodes_df=stations, edges_df=lines, weighted=True, graph_name="Transit")
transit.get_node_df()
```

```{python}
transit.get_edge_df()
```

`nodes_df=` can be left out, in which case the nodes are created from the endpoints in
`edges_df=`. Including it is the way to add isolated nodes and node attributes.

Since Polars reads CSV, Parquet, JSON, databases, and much more, this is the general route for
loading a graph from any tabular source. A typical pattern renames the source's columns to the ones
EdgeCase expects:

```python
edges = pl.read_csv("interactions.csv").rename({"protein_a": "from", "protein_b": "to"})
graph = ec.Graph(edges_df=edges)
```

For graph file formats such as GraphML, GML, or Pajek, see [File formats](file-formats.qmd), and
for other libraries' graph objects, see [Other libraries](other-libraries.qmd).

## Deleting nodes and edges

[`delete_node()`](../reference/Graph.delete_node.qmd) removes a node along with every edge that
touches it:

```{python}
transit.delete_node("Park")
transit.get_edge_df()
```

[`delete_edge()`](../reference/Graph.delete_edge.qmd) removes an edge, given by its endpoints or by
its ID (`id=`), and leaves both endpoints in place. When several parallel edges join the same two
nodes, deleting by endpoints removes only the first of them, so use
[`delete_edge_by_id()`](../reference/Graph.delete_edge_by_id.qmd) to remove a particular one:

```{python}
transit.delete_edge("Central", "Harbour")
transit.get_edges_str_repr()
```

To delete many nodes or edges that meet some condition, select them first and then call
`delete_nodes_ws()` or `delete_edges_ws()`, as shown in [Selections](selections.qmd).

## Cleaning up

Graphs built from raw data often contain self-loops and repeated edges, either by accident or
because the data records repeated events. Some algorithms assume a simple graph, and repeated edges
inflate degrees and other counts. Here is a graph with both problems:

```{python}
messy = (
    ec.Graph()
    .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"])
    .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("A", "B"), ("B", "B"), ("B", "C")])
)
messy.which_multiple(), messy.which_loops()
```

[`which_multiple()`](../reference/Graph.which_multiple.qmd) returns the IDs of the parallel edges
and [`which_loops()`](../reference/Graph.which_loops.qmd) the IDs of the self-loops, which helps to
inspect them before removing anything. Three methods do the removal:

- [`remove_selfloops()`](../reference/Graph.remove_selfloops.qmd) deletes every self-loop.
- [`remove_duplicate_edges()`](../reference/Graph.remove_duplicate_edges.qmd) keeps the first edge
  (the one with the lowest ID) between each pair of nodes. With `keep_distinct_attributes=True`,
  it only merges edges whose attributes are all equal.
- [`simplify()`](../reference/Graph.simplify.qmd) does both.

```{python}
messy.simplify()
messy.is_simple(), messy.get_edges_str_repr()
```

In a directed graph, `A -> B` and `B -> A` are different pairs, so reciprocal edges survive
`remove_duplicate_edges()`. To turn them into a single undirected edge, convert the graph with
`to_undirected()`, described in [Transforming graphs](transforming.qmd).

## Combining construction methods

The methods on this page compose with the generators of the next page, which also add to an
existing graph rather than creating a new one. This builds a small graph by hand, adds a ring of
generated nodes, and wires the two together:

```{python}
combined = (
    ec.Graph()
    .add_node("center")
    .add_cycle_graph(n=5, label=False)
    .add_edges_by_id([(1, node) for node in range(2, 7)])
)
combined.plot(label_by="id", seed=3)
```

The cycle's five nodes were created without labels (`label=False`) and received IDs 2 to 6, after
the hub's ID 1, so `add_edges_by_id()` can join them to the hub by ID. The result is a wheel. The
[generators](generators.qmd) page has much more on building graphs like this.
